overall_summary: Space-themed content focusing on extreme planetary anomalies and bizarre cosmic physics consistently outperforms other niches like psychology and general biology. Repetitive posting of identical brain-fact concepts leads to severe audience fatigue and algorithmic suppression.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice' (1,055 views), 'The Planet Darker Than Coal' (987 views), and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (634 views) represent the top tier of performance.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on extreme exoplanet characteristics, focusing on highly visual, mind-bending physical properties (extreme heat, bizarre rain, massive scale).

winning_patterns.evidence: 'What Does Outer Space Actually Smell Like?' (368 views) and 'Sharks Are Older Than Trees?' (302 views) perform significantly better than abstract facts.
winning_patterns.action: Frame cosmic or historical facts using familiar sensory anchors (smell, taste, common objects like trees) to make the scale immediately relatable.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' was posted three times, yielding only 5, 7, and 53 views respectively. 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' got only 17 views.
weak_patterns.action: Retire generic brain and memory facts. If psychology is used, it must feature a highly unusual historical experiment or a shocking, non-cliché phenomenon.

weak_patterns.pattern: Abstract Cosmic Concepts Lacking Visual Contrast
weak_patterns.evidence: 'This Star Is Older Than the Universe!' (11 views) and 'The Star Colder Than Ice' (79 views) failed to capture interest compared to physical planets.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid purely chronological or temperature-based abstract stellar facts unless they can be paired with a highly dramatic visual comparison.

next_video.concept: J1407b (Super Saturn) and what Earth's sky would look like if it replaced Saturn.
next_video.opening_direction: If this planet replaced Saturn, its rings would look 100 times wider than the full moon in our night sky.
next_video.twist_direction: But these rings are so massive they are actually a cosmic vacuum, violently pulling in nearby space debris to birth new moons.
next_video.reason: Leverages the highly successful exoplanet anomaly pattern. By focusing on J1407b's extreme ring scale and using a 'what-if' Earth comparison, it combines visual scale with cosmic physics, matching the performance profile of the channel's top-performing space videos.

experiment: Test a 'What-If' visual simulation format where we compare Earth's sky with different cosmic anomalies (e.g., if a black hole replaced the moon) to see if the visual comparison increases average view duration.
